title: the visitor who came at night
hook: the altar call at camp, and a phrase that's older than any altar call
carry: never too old to start again
tomorrow: under the water and back up

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Trinity, three and still one. Today, a phrase you've heard about people, and maybe about yourself.

The music slows down. Every head bowed, every eye closed. The speaker says: if you want to give your life to Jesus tonight, raise your hand, or come forward. Some people walked down that aisle at summer camp, some in a stadium, some never did. The phrase people used afterward was born again. That phrase is much older than any altar call. It comes from a conversation at night.

A respected teacher named Nicodemus comes to Jesus after dark. Jesus tells him: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word for again, anothen, has a second meaning: from above. Nicodemus hears the first one and asks the obvious question: "How can a man be born when he is old?" Climb back into the womb? Jesus means the second: a birth from above, by God's Spirit, which he compares to the wind. You can't see where it comes from; you only hear it. A few lines later comes the verse on the signs at football games, John 3:16: "For God so loved the world." The altar call itself is much newer. Revival preachers in the 1800s began inviting people to come forward, and big stadium crusades made it famous. Ask Jesus into your heart isn't a Bible phrase either; it's a simple way churches put it. And churches differ on how new birth happens: in a moment of decision, in baptism, over a lifetime. But notice the picture Jesus chose. Nobody gives birth to themselves.
screen: `A TEACHER, AFTER DARK.` · `ANOTHEN — AGAIN, FROM ABOVE.` · `LIKE THE WIND.` · `THE ALTAR CALL CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of something in your life that feels tired or stuck. On the second, notice you can't force it to be new, any more than a baby can give birth to itself. On the third, just leave a little room for something new to come.
Born again. In the Greek of the story, born from above, too. Third word.
Your line: never too old to start again. It answers the question Nicodemus asked that night. That's day three.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: UNDER THE WATER AND BACK UP.`

howItsDone: Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians describe being born again as a moment of turning to Christ, sometimes at an altar call or by praying a short prayer; Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and other churches connect new birth closely with baptism and a lifelong turning toward God.

original.note: Greek: again, anew, or from above. Jesus's word to Nicodemus carries both.

trapdoor: what you thought: a type of Christian, or a moment at an altar.
what it means: a new birth that comes from God, the way no one gives birth to themselves.
what a scholar hears: anothen in John 3:3 means both 'again' and 'from above'; Nicodemus hears the first, Jesus means the second. the altar call grew from early-1800s revivals (the 'anxious bench').

story.title: the man who came back in daylight
story.text: Jesus has been executed, and most of his friends have scattered. A man walks up to the cross carrying about a hundred pounds of spices for the burial, far more than anyone needs. It's Nicodemus, the teacher who once came only after dark. With another man, Joseph, he wraps the body in linen and lays it in a new tomb. The Gospel never says what changed in him. It just shows him, in the open, when it cost something.

wrong.myth: ask Jesus into your heart is a line from the Bible.
wrong.truth: it's a church way of saying it. the Bible's phrase, from a conversation at night, is born again, which in Greek can also mean born from above.

build.prompt: the Greek word anothen means two things. build both.

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06), written from the audience research: the altar call and 'accepting Jesus into your heart' (top-20 moment 3, proposed day 3), taught through John 3 so the doctrine rests on a scene people can picture.
Sensitive: some listeners have painful memories of altar calls. The hook describes the moment without praising or mocking it; the practice asks nothing of anyone. Please read for tone.

Altar call history stated as 'revival preachers in the 1800s began inviting people to come forward, and big stadium crusades made it famous'. Methodist camp-meeting 'mourner's benches' (c. 1800) and Finney's 'anxious bench' (1820s–30s) are the usual origin points; no named living preacher. Confirm.
'Ask Jesus into your heart isn't a Bible phrase': the phrase is a paraphrase drawing on texts like Ephesians 3:17 and Revelation 3:20. Confirm the wording is fair and not dismissive.
How new birth happens: decision (many evangelicals), baptism (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and others), lifelong (many). Kept to one sentence; confirm.
Story card: Nicodemus brings 'about a hundred pound weight' of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Confirm the telling.
John 3:16 is the one text named in the spoken lines; the football-sign image is general, with no named person.
